englishScript:
Śrī Bhagavān Uvāca |
Imaṁ Vivasvate Yogaṁ Proktavān Aham Avyayam |
Vivasvān Manave Prāha Manur Ikṣvākave 'bravīt || 4-1 ||
translation: The Blessed Lord said: I taught this imperishable Yoga to Vivasvan; Vivasvan declared it to Manu; Manu proclaimed it to Ikshvaku.
explanationSentences: Paragraph 1 explores the foundational principles of the ancient lineage of knowledge (parampara) within the framework of Jnana Karma Sanyasa Yoga.
In this verse, krishna explains the timeless disciplic lineage through which wisdom flows down.
Think of a high-tech solar power station where sunlight is converted into electrical energy and transmitted across regional grids.
If the transmission cables are kept clean and well-insulated, maximum electrical horsepower reaches every town along the route.
If the cables rust or break due to long neglect, the town falls into darkness despite the sun shining brightly above.
Your mind and learning habits operate like those transmission cables when you receive knowledge from mentors and books.
When you maintain a clear, uncorrupted channel of inquiry (*Pariprashna*), knowledge flows into your working memory effortlessly.
Most students believe that true understanding is a secret gift reserved only for a few genetically lucky individuals.
However, first-principles deduction proves that wisdom is a universal science accessible to any mind that cleans its filters.
Jnana Yoga teaches you to burn away false assumptions using the blazing fire of objective knowledge (*Jnana-Agni*).
Consider how a skilled blacksmith places a cold piece of rusted iron into a hot furnace fire.
The intense heat burns away the rust, softens the metal, and allows the smith to hammer it into a sharp, useful tool.
Your mental doubt and performance anxiety are that rusted iron waiting to be purified in your daily study furnace.
When you ignite the fire of intense curiosity, your confusion burns to ashes, leaving pure logical clarity.
You gain total access to your prefrontal executive control, enabling zero-error calculation and rapid problem-solving.
Notice how Krishna highlights the importance of asking sharp questions (*Pariprashna*) with humble openness (*Pranipata*).
Never hide your confusion out of pride or fear of looking foolish in front of peers or instructors.
Saying 'I do not understand this yet' is the mandatory first step that opens your mind to breakthrough insights.
